paper_title: On the Generalization Limitation of On-Policy Distillation for Post-RL Consolidation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends on-policy distillation (OPD) to consolidate capabilities from multiple teachers. Although prior work reports near-perfect in-distribution (IND) distillation performance, we find that this can mask incomplete capability consolidation beyond the supervised distribution. A preliminary study on synthetic reasoning shows that OPD does not fully transfer teachers' generalization capabilities. We then extend this investigation to real-world tasks, evaluating extrapolative and compositional generalization across mathematical reasoning, coding, agent, and long-context capabilities using Qwen3 models. Across extrapolative settings, OPD and MOPD reach 96.04-102.73% of their teachers' IND scores. Yet their out-of-distribution (OOD) scores remain 2.45-16.25% below the base model's. Across three compositional settings, MOPD improves IND performance over the base model, but its performance on composed tasks as OOD remains 18.19-24.34% below that of the best teachers. To understand these gaps, we examine teacher capability and data coverage as two potential bottlenecks. Jointly alleviating these bottlenecks eliminates OOD forgetting in our experiments and suggests the potential for generalization beyond the teacher. (M)OPD also reduces OOD forgetting on average relative to its reinforcement learning (RL) baselines. Analysis of the associated update geometry reveals smaller and more spectrally concentrated updates on average than those of the RL baselines, along with greater shared update structure under MOPD. Motivated by these findings, we propose geometry-based patching and base-preserving replay to improve OOD performance while largely preserving IND performance. Our findings identify a blind spot in capability consolidation via (M)OPD, highlighting the need for algorithms that explicitly support OOD retention and generalization.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains student model on its own generated trajectories using supervision from teacher [1, 40]. Its extension, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), offers way to consolidate capabilities from separately trained teachers into one model [41]. This approach is used as consolidation stage in large-scale post-training pipelines to combine domain-specialized teachers [9, 11, 28, 44], achieving strong distillation performance. The intended outcome of post-RL consolidation is to learn the teachers improvements while retaining the base models capabilities and supporting their use beyond the supervised tasks. We find that achieving near1 perfect in-distribution (IND) distillation does not reliably yield either out-of-distribution (OOD) retention or OOD generalization beyond the base. Near-perfect IND distillation can therefore mask incomplete capability consolidation. We start from preliminary study on synthetic reasoning task ( 4, Power et al. [50], Zhang et al. [64]) to illustrate the generalization limitation of OPD. The self-RL teacher and OPD student start from common pretrained base. When the teacher generalizes beyond the supervised range, OPD does not fully transfer that generalization despite strong IND performance. This motivates testing whether the same limitation persists when consolidating capabilities on real-world tasks, where useful behavior can extend far beyond narrow distillation data and require distinct capabilities together. Our main experiments use Qwen3-based models [59] to study two forms of generalization across mathematical reasoning, coding, agent, and long-context capabilities ( 3). Extrapolative generalization tests performance beyond the supervised range within capability [4, 64], using mathematical reasoning benchmarks of differing difficulty. Compositional generalization tests whether separately supervised capabilities can be used together [30, 63]. We also distinguish two teacher setups: self-RL specialist teachers are independently trained from common base and then distilled into student initialized from the same base, reflecting specialization followed by consolidation; external generalist teachers are obtained separately and used to distill stronger capabilities into smaller student ( 3.1). First, across both teacher setups, near-perfect IND distillation coexists with OOD forgetting ( 5). Across individual training datasets and mixtures, OPD and MOPD reach 96.04-102.73% of their teachers mean IND scores, yet their mean OOD scores remain 2.45-16.25% below the base. The gap persists even with stronger external generalist teacher that outperforms the base model on OOD evaluations. Second, component improvements do not ensure compositional generalization ( 6). Across the three settings, MOPD improves mean IND performance by 0.48-22.46% over the base but remains 18.19-24.34% below the best teachers on composed tasks. For example, in code plus long context, MOPD improves all three component benchmarks, yet on the composed task (long-context coding) it is still at about the bases performance level, below both teachers. Improvements on separately supervised component tasks therefore need not translate into gains on tasks requiring those capabilities to be combined. To understand these gaps, we examine teacher capability and data coverage as two potential bottlenecks to OOD performance. Jointly alleviating these bottlenecks eliminates OOD forgetting in our experiments and suggests the potential for generalization beyond the teacher ( 7.1). Despite the remaining gaps, our main experiments also show that OPD and MOPD reduce average OOD forgetting relative to the self-RL teachers and mixed RL, respectively. To examine the associated parameter changes, we draw on analyses of multi-task training and OPD geometry [53, 68]. (M)OPD produces smaller and more spectrally concentrated updates on average than their corresponding RL baselines. Moreover, across both generalization settings, MOPD updates are better explained by the span of single-teacher OPD updates than mixed-RL updates are by the span of single-RL updates ( 7.2). Appendix provides complementary local theoretical analysis. Motivated by the observed update structure, we investigate geometry-based patching after distillation. Patching partially closes the OOD gap on AIME25 while retaining most of the teachers IND performance. We also investigate base-preserving replay to explicitly preserve the base models behavior during distillation ( 8). Relative to plain OPD, replay improves scores on five of eight OOD benchmarks with only small decrease in IND performance, and surpasses both the student base and RL teacher on AIME25. Overall, near-perfect IND distillation can mask incomplete capability consolidation, motivating explicit support for OOD retention and generalization.

sections.title: 2.1 On-Policy Distillation and Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation
sections.content: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains student on trajectories sampled from its own policy, using the teachers next-token predictions as supervision [1, 40]. It combines the nature of on-policy state distribution, like reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), with the dense token-level supervision signal of knowledge distillation [19, 52]. Prior work reports strong distillation of teacher performance and rapid convergence in mathematical reasoning, knowledge question answering [40], and multi-turn agentic tasks [35, 56]. Multiteacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends this approach by assigning training domains to teachers with corresponding capabilities [41]. It is increasingly used for post-RL consolidation in frontier model development: domain experts are trained separately and then distilled into single student [9, 11, 28, 44], showing great distillation performance. Much of the methodological work [24, 56, 57] aims to improve target-task performance in domain. However, we suggest that this near-perfect distillation performance can be limited in IND evaluation. We complement these studies by focusing on OOD performance, suggesting that it can conceal incomplete generalization. Two recent studies are close to ours but different. Gao et al. [14] diagnose capability conflict and imbalance in MOPD, but the capabilities are all within the training distribution (i.e., IND). Li et al. [34] examine generalization across domains (e.g., from math to science) or across languages, which differs from our generalization forms; it is more about the closeness of different tasks but not the algorithms potential.

sections.title: 2.2 Generalization in Post-Training
sections.content: Generalization is models ability to perform well on examples out of the training distribution. Grokking demonstrates that generalization on algorithmic datasets emerges long after model fits the training data [50]. Studies on modular arithmetic also show that models can generalize to tasks requiring skill composition [17]. In LLM post-training, RLVR can improve reasoning on the training domain while producing inconsistent gains on unseen domains [13, 20, 63, 64]. These findings motivate treating rapid IND convergence and OOD generalization as separate empirical questions. Although OPD can approach teacher performance within relatively few updates [40], such convergence alone does not establish whether the student inherits the teachers generalization. We hence study whether (M)OPD transfers performance beyond the supervised distribution.

sections.title: 2.3 Capability Consolidation
sections.content: Capability consolidation aims to combine multiple capabilities in single model, often at the final stage of posttraining. Established approaches include model merging and mixed RL. Model merging combines separately trained models directly in parameter space [3, 22, 58, 60, 61]. Mixed RL jointly optimizes single model on data from multiple tasks using their corresponding rewards [31, 59]. On another thread, related work studies relationships among capabilities, for example, by pairwise transfer and latent factors in transfer matrices [26, 29] or by using sparse autoencoder features [12]. Our evaluations ask whether consolidation preserves performance beyond the supervised distribution, generalizing to tasks requiring multiple capabilities together.

Specialist teachers primarily improve their target capabilities but may exhibit forgetting on others [15]. sections.title: 3.2 IND Performance and Two Forms of Generalization
sections.content: We define the in-distribution (IND) evaluations relative to the distributions directly supervised during distillation. Out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluations probe distributions or combinations of capabilities outside that supervision. In multi-teacher experiments, the supervised distribution includes the data supplied by all teachers. For the cross-benchmark mathematical aggregates, we operationalize this grouping using the self-RL teachers performance relative to the base; the criterion and its limitations are given in A.2.1. Extrapolative generalization. We evaluate performance beyond the range covered by the supervised distribution, such as more complex problems within the same domain. We separately measure OOD retention, meaning maintenance of the base models OOD performance, and OOD generalization, meaning improvement beyond the base on OOD evaluations. Incomplete transfer of teachers positive OOD improvement and students loss relative to the base are distinct possible outcomes. Compositional generalization. We train on data for separate component capabilities and evaluate on tasks requiring their combination. We compare the student with the base and both teachers. Improvement over the base establishes benefit on the composed task; surpassing both teachers would provide stronger evidence that consolidation yields an additional benefit from combining their capabilities. We report component and composed-task evaluations separately.

sections.title: 3.3 Training Data and Evaluation Benchmarks
sections.content: For mathematical reasoning, we train on GSM8K [8], MATH [18], and DAPO [62], and evaluate on GSM8K, MATH500 [36], AMC23 [2], and AIME24/25 [21, 46]. For coding, we train on Nemotron competitive-coding data [43] and evaluate on HumanEval [7], MBPP [5], and their EvalPlus extensions [37]. For agent capabilities, we train on synthetic BFCL live/non-live data [48], xLAM60K [39], and ToolACE [38], and evaluate primarily on BFCL V4s non-live and live subsets. For long context, we train on DocQA-RL-1.6K (DocQA) [55] and evaluate on LongBench-v2 [6], primarily its Hard subset. We mainly probe extrapolative generalization through mathematical reasoning, using shifts from narrow training distributions such as GSM8K to harder benchmarks such as AIME24/25. This follows prior work evaluating mathematical reasoning beyond the training difficulty [10, 20, 32, 34, 42]. We test compositional generalization through long-context math reasoning 4 on GSM-Infinite [67] and DocMath [65], long-context coding on LongBench-v2 Code, and agentic coding on SWE-bench Verified [25]. Per-run data assignments, evaluation subsets, and scoring protocols are detailed in A.2 and A.3.

sections.title: 4 Preliminary Study: Strong IND Performance Leaves an OOD Gap
sections.content: OPD can achieve near-perfect IND distillation within relatively few training steps [40, 41]. Yet grokking shows that generalization can emerge long after model fits its training data [50]. This motivates asking whether rapid IND convergence in OPD is accompanied by transfer of the teachers generalization. We examine this question in controlled synthetic mathematical reasoning study. Settings. Following the framework of Zhang et al. [64], we pretrain randomly initialized Qwen2-100M model on GSM-Infinite-based problems [67] requiring 2-10 operations to obtain the base checkpoint π0. We then train self-RL teacher from π0 on problems requiring 11-14 operations. The OPD student starts from the same base π0 and learns from this teacher on the same post-training data distribution. In this controlled study, we report the pretraining range (2-10 operations) and post-training range (1114) separately as IND evaluations; 15-17 operations test OOD extrapolation beyond both ranges. Operation count provides an explicit axis of difficulty before we turn to post-training experiments on realworld tasks. Figure 1 Near-perfect IND distillation leaves an OOD transfer gap. The distillation ratio is sstudentsbase , where steachersbase is acc@1 at each operation count. Pretraining IND covers 2-10 operations, post-training IND covers 11-14, and OOD covers 15-17. The dashed line marks complete transfer of the teachers improvement over the base. Findings. Figure 1 shows near-perfect IND distillation alongside incomplete OOD transfer. While the distillation ratio of OPD is approximately 96-104% on pretraining IND and 93-96% on post-training IND, it falls to 76-86% on OOD problems. Thus, when the teacher generalizes beyond the supervised range, OPD does not fully transfer that generalization despite strong IND performance. This motivates testing whether the same limitation persists when consolidating capabilities on real-world tasks, where useful behavior can extend far beyond narrow distillation data and require distinct capabilities together.

sections.title: 5 Strong IND Performance Does Not Ensure Extrapolative Generalization
sections.content: We examine whether near-perfect IND distillation yields extrapolative generalization in mathematical reasoning, using self-RL specialist teachers and external generalist teachers. Overall findings. Across both teacher setups, near-perfect IND distillation coexists with OOD forgetting. OPD and MOPD reduce average forgetting relative to the self-RL teachers and mixed RL, respectively, but still fall below the base on OOD evaluations.

sections.title: 5.1 Self-RL Specialist Teachers
sections.content: Single-teacher OPD. OPD achieves near-perfect IND distillation, reaching 97.10% of its teachers IND score on average across all three training datasets (Figure 2). Yet its OOD performance decreases relative to the base by 10.78% (8.56 percentage points). 1 We find that the three self-RL teachers also exhibit OOD forgetting, similar results reported in Li et al. These labels describe compatibility with the teachers post-training regime rather than establish distributional membership or pretraining exposure; see A.2.1. 5 Figure 2 Near-perfect IND distillation does not ensure OOD retention. Within each panel, benchmarks are arranged from IND on the left to OOD on the right. On most OOD evaluations, OPD performance (purple solid lines) lies between the base (gray dashed lines) and the corresponding teacher (gray solid lines), indicating reduced but persistent forgetting. In this experiment, teachers themselves also exhibit OOD forgetting, scoring below the base. 5.2 further shows that OPD forgetting persists even with an external generalist teacher that outperforms the base on OOD. Results cover all pairwise and three-teacher mixtures; AIME scores report avg@8. OPD reduces average OOD forgetting by 25.09% relative to its self-RL teachers: the mean loss from the base falls from 11.43 to 8.56 percentage points. Overall, near-perfect IND distillation does not ensure OOD improvement over the base. 7.2 examines the parameter-update differences accompanying OPDs milder forgetting. Nevertheless, MOPD reduces average OOD forgetting by 28.92% relative to mixed RL, whose mean loss from the base is 15.73 points.

sections.title: 5.2 External Generalist Teachers
sections.content: To test whether the gaps depend on teacher-side forgetting, we use an external generalist teacher that is not obtained by specializing the student base through our self-RL pipeline. Specifically, we distill Qwen3-32B into Qwen3-8B (Figure 4). The teacher model generally outperforms the student base across most evaluations. This setup therefore makes stronger OOD performance available for transfer on OOD tasks like AIME. Across the three distillation datasets, OPD achieves near-perfect IND distillation, reaching 99.34% of the teachers IND score (0.62 points below it), yet remains 3.73% below the base on OOD evaluations (2.96 points). Stronger teacher performance alone therefore does not ensure OOD transfer or retention under narrow supervision. 7.1 further examines whether broader distillation data improves these outcomes. 6 Figure 4 stronger external teacher does not eliminate OOD gaps. Qwen3-32B teaches Qwen3-8B; AIME scores report avg@8. All three figures use the same Qwen3-8B base scores.

sections.title: 6 Component Improvements Do Not Ensure Compositional Generalization
sections.content: We next ask whether MOPD can consolidate separate capabilities to benefit tasks requiring their combination, i.e., compositional generalization. Specifically, we study code plus agent, math plus long context, and code plus long context. The desired outcome is student that learns both components and surpasses its teacher or teachers on the composed task. In the experiments, MOPD assigns an external teacher to each components training data. For comparison, we construct mixed RL from single-task recipes, including training data, that achieve component performance comparable to MOPD. Both methods use the same fixed mixture proportions and random shuffling without further tuning to balance tasks for fair comparison. Overall findings. Across the three settings, MOPD improves IND performance by 9.24% over the base (3.97% below the corresponding teachers), but remains 23.82% below the best teachers on composed tasks (Figures 5 to 7). Mixed RL shows similar compositional gap (26.10%); MOPDs mean composed-task score is 3.08% (1.07 percentage points) higher than mixed RLs. Code and Agent. Coding and tool-use supervision improves SWE-bench Verified from the bases 6.63 to 8.05, above mixed RL (7.79) but below the shared teacher (9.84; Figure 5). MOPD also improves over the base on all component benchmarks except HumanEval+. IND scores average HumanEval, HumanEval+, and BFCL-v4 Non-live/Live. MOPD outperforms mixed RL on SWE-bench Verified and three of four IND evaluations. Math and Long Context. MOPD improves LongBench-v2 from 40.50 to 56.20 and GSM8K from 83.40 to 95.53, yet the composed-task outcomes diverge (Figure 6). DocMath improves from 55.38 to 60.63, whereas GSMInfinite falls from 50.88 to 49.75; both remain below the best teacher. MOPD nevertheless outperforms mixed RL on all displayed benchmarks. Code and Long Context. MOPD improves all three component benchmarks, yet LongBench-v2 Code remains at the bases 44.00, below both teachers (50.00 and 58.00; Figure 7). Mixed RL raises this composed-task score to 46.00 but lowers the LongBench-v2 component score from 40.50 to 38.84, illustrating trade-off between component retention and composed-task performance. 7 Figure 6 Compositional generalization to long-context math: MOPD reaches 96.0% of the teachers mean IND score but remains 24.3% below the best teacher on composed tasks. The code plus agent, math plus long-context, and code plus long-context evaluations show compositional generalization limitation: student can acquire improvements on separately supervised capabilities without obtaining the expected performance when those capabilities must be combined.

sections.title: 7.1 Teacher Capability and Data Coverage Contribute to OOD Gaps
sections.content: Under narrow supervision, students can remain below the base model on OOD evaluations with either self-RL specialists ( 5.1) or stronger external generalists ( 5.2). Thus, stronger teacher capability alone is insufficient for OOD retention (panels a-b of Figure 8). To relax both bottlenecks (panel c), we keep Qwen3-32B as teacher and train on 90% GSM8K plus 10% OpenR1 [45]. Compared with GSM8K-only distillation, it exceeds the base on all five benchmarks. The student matches the teachers AIME24/25 pass@8 (86.67/83.33). On AMC23, it improves to 100.00, exceeding the teachers 95.00 (Figure 9). Together, these results suggest considering teacher capability and data coverage jointly (Figure 8): stronger teacher makes OOD capabilities available, while broader supervision helps the student retain or acquire them. Easing both bottlenecks can reduce OOD forgetting and potentially encourage further generalization. 8 Figure 8 Teacher capability (A) and data coverage (B) as bottlenecks. We use the flask [54] as an analogy: lower/upper vessels denote teacher/student, and neck width denotes training data coverage. Teal/red bars illustrate qualitative gains/losses relative to the base. (a) Vanilla: The student exhibits less OOD forgetting than its teacher but remains below the base. (b) Relax A: stronger teacher provides positive OOD gains, yet narrow distillation data still leaves the student below the base. (c) Relax A+B: Combining the stronger teacher with broader data coverage can turn student OOD losses into gains. Figure 9 Broader data eliminates OOD forgetting. With Qwen3-32B supervision on GSM8K with 10% OpenR1 additional data to broaden the distribution, the Qwen3-8B student matches the teachers AIME pass@8, surpasses it on AMC23, and exceeds the base on all five benchmarks. AIME reports pass@8; other benchmarks report accuracy.

For each model, we measure its update relative to the common base, = W0. 7.2.1 (M)OPD Produces More Compact Updates than (Mixed) RL Both OPD and MOPD produce smaller updates on average than their corresponding RL baselines  (Table 1)  . Across the extrapolative experiments, at approximately matched IND performance, OPDs update norm is 55.4% of RLs (0.154 versus 0.278). For MOPD, the mean update norm is also smaller than that of mixed RL. OPD updates are also more spectrally concentrated. sections.title: 7.2.2 MOPD Shares More Structure with Single-Teacher Updates
sections.content: For each mixture, we project the MOPD update onto the span of the corresponding single-teacher OPD updates and the mixed-RL update onto the span of the corresponding single-RL updates. We measure the explained fraction of each updates squared norm, R2 = 1 (cid:98)2 , where (cid:98) is the least-squares projection. MOPD is better explained by the single-OPD span than mixed RL is by the single-RL span. The respective spans explain 11.0-18.6% of MOPDs squared update norm and less than 0.240% of mixed RLs  (Table 1)  . Using the same single-RL teacher span for both methods also yields higher R2 for MOPD than for mixed RL. These measurements suggest that MOPD is an algorithm with more shared update structure. /2 Discussion. Mergeability offers perspective on capability consolidation. Understanding which models and capabilities can be merged successfully, and with which algorithms, remains an open question. The literature considers factors including update direction [22], weight disentanglement [47], parameter-wise sign conflicts [58], and subspace and gradient alignment [66]. Our observations of smaller (M)OPD updates and greater shared update structure with single-teacher OPD motivate hypothesis: compact updates may limit disruption to component capabilities, providing more favorable conditions for compositional generalization after capability consolidation. This perspective also motivates model-merging-style editing to improve OOD performance after distillation ( 8.1). Appendix provides complementary local theoretical analysis. Please note that these connections remain preliminary interpretation. causal link between these geometric properties and generalization has yet to be established.

sections.title: 8 Exploring Patching Methods for Mitigating OOD Gap
sections.content: Since near-perfect IND distillation can coexist with an OOD performance gap, improving generalization also requires preserving capabilities beyond the training distribution. We investigate two explicit interventions: geometry-based patching after distillation and base-preserving replay during distillation.

sections.title: 8.2 Base-Preserving Replay
sections.content: KL-regularized RLVR constrains policy drift from reference model [52]. In contrast, the (M)OPD objectives in 3.1 match task teachers without an explicit constraint to preserve the base models behavior. We hypothesize that this missing constraint contributes to OOD forgetting. Motivated by replay methods for capability preservation during RL post-training [49], we introduce base-preserving replay for (M)OPD. Base-preserving replay mixes IND examples supervised by the task teachers with additional prompts supervised by the base model, using the same OPD loss. We test coding and instruction-following data as replay sources outside the specialists mathematical training distribution; Figure 11 reports coding replay for the GSM8K OPD student distilled from self-RL teacher. Figure 11 Base-preserving replay improves five of eight OOD scores over plain OPD with small IND change, and surpasses both the student base and RL teacher on AIME25. AIME scores report avg@8. Relative to plain OPD, coding replay improves five of eight OOD scores, including 6.67-point increase in AIME25 avg@8 to 67.50, surpassing both the student base and RL teacher with only 0.18-point reduction in GSM8K accuracy. These results suggest that replay can support both retention and generalization beyond the replay domain.

sections.title: 9.1 Limitations
sections.content: Our main post-training experiments are on Qwen3-8B students, and our largest external teacher is Qwen3-32B given computation constraints. Fixing the student supports within-model comparisons, but leaves dependence on student capacity, teacher strength, and model family under-explored. We have preliminarily tested self-RL specialist extrapolative generalization on Qwen3-235B-A22B on smaller scale. In that run, we do not see the generalization limitation as minor as size scales. Public datasets make our comparisons inspectable, but do not reproduce the breadth or adaptive data selection of full post-training pipelines in frontier model development. Our OOD labels are relative to post-training data, not pretraining exposure. Broader training data from the real world and held-out evaluations with graded difficulty would test generalization under more demanding conditions. Mixed RL and MOPD both combine component recipes without extensive tuning of reward balancing, mixture weights, or curricula ( A.1). They may not establish each objectives best achievable performance. However, we have tuned hyperparameters for single OPD and single RL recipes to ensure optimal performance. Given the much larger tuning space for Mixed RL and MOPD, we treat the current settings as out-of-the-box usage and still fair comparison. We leave these additional tunings as further work. Our main findings on the relative performance of MOPD and mixed RL concern the tested LLM architecture and practical post-training tasks. At the algorithmic level, this ordering need not hold for simpler models and tasks with different generalization requirements, which we additionally discuss in 9.2. Computational constraints prevent us from repeating every experiment with multiple sampling seeds. For mathematical reasoning, we repeat evaluation with four sampling seeds on 10% subset of the evaluation questions and observe consistent qualitative conclusions across these checks. These checks assess variability in sampled responses; they do not establish robustness across independent training runs.

sections.title: 9.2 Scope of MOPD’s Advantage over Mixed RL
sections.content: Our study focuses on empirical performance in practical post-training tasks, rather than establishing universal ordering between MOPD and mixed RL. To be more careful, the advantage observed in 6 is conditional on the evaluated models, training data, and tasks. Task learnability for given model may affect this comparison. Conceptually, MOPD learns from teacher distributions without an independent correctness signal, whereas RL uses verifier feedback on its training tasks. This distinction suggests that mixed RL may outperform MOPD when the model can learn effectively from verifier feedback, even if the teachers remain imperfect. We examine this possibility in controlled synthetic arithmetic setting where the chosen model can achieve perfect accuracy on the target compositions under direct supervision. The controlled synthetic arithmetic experiment run on 3-layer Transformer model provides an example (Figure 12; setup in C). We design an easier generalization task that the model of given size can converge to high performance. Models first train on operators and and their repetitions, with AB and BA held out from both MOPD and mixed RL. We design the task and model architecture that direct SFT on AB/BA reaches 100% accuracy, establishing learnability under direct supervision. In the displayed run, both MOPD variants from warm-RL teachers improve rapidly and then remain around 80-90% composed-task accuracy within the observed training budget, while mixed warm RL later surpasses them. The five-seed final results support this finding. These results reveal that, considering different model architectures, task learnability, interference between tasks, etc., there can be different balances between component performance and compositional generalization. Isolating their effects across architectures and training objectives remains future work. Our main conclusions concern the LLMs and practical post-training tasks.

sections.title: 9.3 Future Work
sections.content: The connection between update geometry, OOD retention, and compositional generalization remains hypothesis. Causal tests should manipulate update directions while controlling update magnitude, training budget, and IND performance. Beyond post-hoc patching, step-level parameter-space control could project or regularize updates during training, with random-direction controls. Future work should also jointly study teacher assignment, data coverage, and base-preserving replay under fixed budget, testing retention and further generalization beyond expanded training coverage. sections.content: A.1 Training and Teacher Assignment Self-RL specialists and their OPD students start independently from the same Qwen3-8B base. Each specialist supervises its own training distribution. External teachers are Qwen3-32B for mathematical reasoning, QwenLong-L1.5-30B-A3B for long context, and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 for coding and tool use. Code plus agent uses one shared teacher; the other composed settings use separate teachers for the two components. We select external teachers from pool of open-source Qwen3-family models (including domain-specific models) and fine-tuned models released on Hugging Face that are based on them, with compatible vocabularies for token-level distillation. Among candidates whose sizes fit our compute budget, we choose the best-performing model on the relevant benchmarks under our controlled inference setup. Scores under this setup may differ slightly from published results. In Equation (1), both policies are evaluated at student-generated histories, and the teacher is fixed. Interactive histories include tool observations, but the loss sums only over model-generated tokens. Mixed RL uses the combination of single-task GRPO recipes. The highest mean IND score among evaluated configurations selects each methods recipe and checkpoint. In Mixed RL experiments, the component recipes are selected for IND performance comparable to MOPD, then combined with equal data proportions and random shuffling, without additional tuning of balance. External teachers may have additional prior training. The main extrapolative and compositional generalization experiments use learning rate of 106. (M)OPD mainly uses the k1 distillation loss with policy gradients enabled and task rewards disabled. We smoke test that different distillation loss have non-significant difference in performance after sufficient training steps in our experiments. MOPD selects the teacher by data source. RL uses GRPO with one PPO epoch per update, KL loss coefficient of 0.001, and an entropy coefficient of 0. (M)OPD rollouts in these experiments use temperature 1.0 and top-p 1.0. A.2.1 Operational Definition of IND and OOD For the cross-benchmark mathematical aggregates, we use an operational IND/OOD grouping based on the teachers empirical results to post-training. This choice addresses practical challenge: training corpora assembled from multiple sources and independently constructed evaluation benchmarks need not provide corresponding train/test splits. Evaluating across these benchmarks allows us to examine broader range of post-training settings, while requiring an explicit criterion for grouping their relationships to training. Performance-based, model-relative operationalizations have precedents. Kim et al. [27] define in-distribution questions through models probability of answering correctly, while Guo et al. [16] construct ID/OOD labels from prediction correctness relative to reference models. Jesson et al. [23] similarly use performance to distinguish in-capability and out-of-capability tasks when the pre-training distribution is opaque. These approaches motivate using observable model behavior to characterize task compatibility when distributional membership is difficult to establish. Our specific criterion groups benchmark as IND when each of the three self-RL teachers exceeds 97% of the base models score, identifying evaluations on which performance is improved or largely preserved after teacher training. The remaining benchmarks are grouped as OOD. Thresholds of 95%, 96%, and 98% produce the same partition. This grouping is descriptive proxy for compatibility with the teachers post-training regime. Teacher responses also depend on optimization, interference, and ceiling effects, so the labels do not establish distributional membership or pre-training exposure. Our controlled study in Figure 1 provides complementary evidence using an explicitly specified training range, independently of this performance-based grouping. A.3 Scores and Aggregation AIME avg@8 averages correctness over eight sampled responses per problem; pass@8 counts whether any response is correct. Student/teacher score ratios compare performance, while OOD retention compares the student 22 with the base when teacher is forgetting. For mean OOD forgetting Lm = sbase sm, the reduction relative to reference is 100(Lr Lm)/Lr%. We assess OOD retention and improvement relative to the base, and separately compare the student with the teacher or best participating teacher to assess transfer and any additional benefit from consolidation. Compositional summaries first average the component or composed benchmarks within each setting, then weight the three settings equally. Component references use the assigned teachers; composed-task references use the highest teacher score on each benchmark.
